title: Scaffold packages/pi-subagent, tooling and license
description:
Create the package skeleton. The workspace glob, linter, formatter and test
runner pick it up with no further wiring.

- package.json: name pi-subagent, 0.1.0, type module, engines node >=22,
  pi.extensions ["./src/index.ts"], files ships src/, README and LICENSE.
- Peer the Pi packages at the range the root devDependencies pin, plus
  typebox. Tool parameters must be a typebox TSchema because that is what
  registerTool takes, so typebox is a peer even though Effect is the only
  dependency.
- One runtime dependency: effect, v4.
- tsconfig.json extending ../../tsconfig.base.json.
- LICENSE: MIT, carrying no upstream copyright. This is not a fork of either
  reference extension, it is written against them.

Manifest test, forked from the pi-ask-popup template rather than reused. That
template asserts zero runtime dependencies and this package has one, so the
assertion becomes an exact count. Pin it to 1 and name effect, so adding a
second dependency fails the suite rather than passing unnoticed.

Mutation-check the count assertion before calling this done: add a fake
dependency, watch the test go red, remove it.
close_reason: Package scaffolded. Manifest test pins one runtime dependency, effect. Four assertions mutation-checked: each killed exactly one test.

title: Widget, call preview and result rendering
description:
Three surfaces, all plain Component classes rather than Effect, because Pi's
Component contract is a synchronous render(width) that repaints several times a
second.

The widget sits above the editor, throttled to roughly one render per 150ms,
one line per task: status icon, agent name, tool count, tokens, elapsed, and the
last tool call rendered as a short phrase.

renderCall draws the graph while the model is still typing the call, which is
pi-core-subagent's nicest touch and nearly free. A wave line, then one row per
task showing its id, agent, edges and a truncated goal. Omit the wave line
entirely when no task has needs, so flat work renders flat and the graph
vocabulary is not imposed on work that has no graph.

renderResult is the run summary collapsed, and per-task output expanded.

No peek pane. subagent_result already returns the session file paths, and tail
covers watching one child from another pane.

title: The four tools and their schemas
description:
The parent-facing surface. Every tool here costs context in the orchestrator's
spec on every request, which is the budget this package spends most carefully.
Four, no more.

- subagent. Takes a tasks array, each carrying agent, task and prompt, plus
  optional id, needs, model, thinking and maxTurns. Top-level autoAwait,
  defaulting off. Background by default: the call returns a run id and
  completion notifies.
- subagent_result. The whole run or one task, with wait and verbose. Returns
  each child's session file path, so a run can be watched with tail from
  another pane.
- reply_subagent. Answers a child's ask_parent and resumes it.
- subagent_cancel. Aborts a run.

The tool description and prompt guidelines carry the behaviour the schema
cannot express: batch every sub-task into one call rather than issuing several,
declare ordering with needs rather than by splitting calls, do not restate an
upstream result that the edge already delivers, and end the turn rather than
idling on a background run.

Schemas are typebox, with thinking as a closed enum so the model sees the legal
set instead of guessing at it.

title: Intercom: ask_parent, notify_parent, and the parked queue
description:
The channel pi-subagents does not have, and the reason to build this at all
rather than install that.

ask_parent blocks the child on a Deferred until reply_subagent resolves it, or
until the timeout resolves it with an instruction to proceed on best judgment
and state the assumption made. Every path that ends a task also resolves that
latch: task cancelled, run cancelled, run finalising, session ending. A child
must never be left waiting on a parent that is gone. Under Effect this is a
scope finalizer rather than the same resolve call repeated at six exit points,
which is where both reference implementations spent real care.

notify_parent is one way and does not block.

Parking. While the parent is inside a waiting call, child traffic is collected
rather than sent to the session, and returned inside that tool result. A parent
that is blocked should not have to stop blocking to learn its child asked a
question. Cap the queue, and when it is full let an ask displace the oldest
non-ask, so a blocking question is never dropped in favour of a status update.

The child prompt carries the anti-deadlock instructions, since none of this is
enforced mechanically: an unanswered ask times out, and a gated task in a later
wave is not running yet, so waiting on it will not end.

A task that failed with no output at all is a startup failure, and its notice is
delivered as a steer rather than a follow-up so that it interrupts. The wording
says a config-level error will fail identically on every respawn, so stop and
diagnose rather than retry.
close_reason: Implemented scoped parent intercom with blocking asks, non-blocking notifications, prioritized parked delivery, startup-failure steering, and child tool integration. Mutation checks covered registration order, queue priority, failure routing, and timeout fallback. npm run check passes: 68 files, 1324 tests.

title: Child lifecycle: limits, failure classification, teardown
description:
Running the child, and being honest about how it ended.

Limits. Count turn_end. At the limit, steer "wrap up immediately" once. After
the grace turns, abort. Separately race the whole run against the wall-clock
backstop, which catches a provider call that never returns and that a turn
counter never sees.

Outcomes, each distinct because the parent should act differently on each:
completed, wrapped up at the limit, aborted after grace, timed out, stopped by
the user, and failed.

Failure classification catches two shapes that read as success unless you look
for them. A final assistant message with stopReason "error" is a provider
failure Pi resolved rather than rejecting. A stopReason "length" with no text at
all is a silent output-token death. A "length" stop that did produce text is a
legitimate truncated answer, not a failure. Bound the search to this run's own
messages so a failure never surfaces an earlier turn's answer as if it were
this one's.

Salvage whatever partial output a failed run produced and label it as partial.
Append a status note to any non-normal outcome, phrased as a statement about
state rather than an instruction to act.

Teardown. Emit session_shutdown before dispose. Under Effect this is a scope
finalizer, which is what makes it run on every exit path rather than only the
happy one.

Truncate the returned text at the result cap, measured in bytes, with a footer
naming the child session file so the full transcript stays reachable.
close_reason: Implemented scoped child lifecycle limits, terminal outcomes, output salvage/truncation, and bounded shutdown cleanup

title: Child session: fff-only loading, prompt assembly, tool allowlist
description:
Everything between "the scheduler picked this task" and "the child has a
session".

Extension loading. DefaultResourceLoader with noExtensions true and
additionalExtensionPaths pointing at the installed @ff-labs/pi-fff entry.
Resolve that path rather than hardcoding it, and degrade to no fff rather than
failing the task when it is not installed.

Tool allowlist. Pi's read, grep, find and ls, plus the union of fff's names
across its modes: ffgrep, fffind, fff-multi-grep and multi_grep. grep and find
are already in the list as built-ins, which is exactly what fff's override mode
shadows. fff registers its tools from session_start with a before_agent_start
fallback, not at factory time, so the names have to be in the allowlist up
front: Pi's registration gate is frozen at construction, and a name absent from
it is dropped forever even once the tool actually registers.

Prompt assembly. Pi's base layers, then the inline system prompt, then the
subagent instruction block: you are running as a subagent, your bash already
runs in the project directory so never prefix cd, return a concise final
answer, and here is how to reach the parent.

Call bindExtensions, or fff's session_start never fires and its tools never
register.
close_reason: Implemented isolated persisted child sessions with fff-only loading, frozen read-only tool gating, standalone prompt assembly, exact-name agent files, and async re-entry protection. Real Pi runtime tests prove lazy extension binding and exclusion of write tools; both assertions were mutation-checked. npm run check passes: 66 files, 1299 tests.

title: Run graph: needs validation, wave scheduler, upstream delivery
description:
The scheduler, and the validation that runs before it.

Validation, all at call time so a bad graph costs nothing:

- An unknown task id in needs, a self-edge, and a cycle.
- Duplicate explicit ids, and a generated task id that collides with an
  explicit one.
- Task ids constrained to letters, digits, underscore and hyphen.
- The task count cap.

The scheduler is a wave loop: take every task whose needs are all settled, run
that wave with bounded concurrency, mark them settled, repeat. Single, parallel
and chain are three shapes of that loop, not three code paths.

Upstream delivery builds the dependent's prompt as named output blocks followed
by the task text, substituting the first need's output wherever the task text
asks for the previous result. A task whose need failed is never run: it settles
as skipped, naming the needs that did not complete, rather than running against
a prompt with a hole in it.

Under Effect a wave is Effect.all with a concurrency bound, and the whole run is
a fiber in a scope, so cancelling the run interrupts its children rather than
leaving them to finish unattended.

This is pure logic, so test it directly: wave composition, gating, skip
propagation, and each rejected graph shape. A test that cannot fail is not a
test, so break the cycle check on purpose and watch the right one go red.
close_reason: Landed in packages/pi-subagent/src/graph.ts with 29 tests. One Kahn layering does cycle detection and wave assignment together, which makes gating structural in the scheduler rather than a settled set.

title: Model and thinking resolution, validated before any child spawns
description:
One resolver, used by every spawn path, implementing the precedence recorded in
the ADR: agent file, then settings, then the per-task field, then the parent
model.

Model resolution, combining what the two references each got right:

- Exact provider/modelId against getAvailable() first, so auth is part of
  resolution rather than a later failure.
- A bare id resolves against the session's own provider before anything else. A
  user who types a bare id almost always means the provider they are already
  authenticated to.
- Then fuzzy. Normalize . to - so claude-haiku-4.5 and claude-haiku-4-5 are one
  query, and treat a trailing eight-digit date stamp as optional in both
  directions.
- A provider/modelId that matched nothing under that provider retries the bare
  id across all providers, so the same model elsewhere beats falling back to
  inherit.
- On total failure, return an error listing every available model. The
  orchestrator that guessed wrong should see what it could have picked.

Thinking resolution is getSupportedThinkingLevels(model) and nothing else.

Validation runs over the whole task list before the run exists, so an
unsupported pair fails the call with zero children spawned, and the message
names the task, the agent and the supported set.

Also settle the preflight probe here. pi-core-subagent sends a real 16-token
ping for any model that differs from the session's, and falls back to the
session model with a note when it errors. It costs one tiny request per task
and catches the failure a hand-picked model actually produces: a provider
configured once whose key has since expired. Land it or record why not.
close_reason: Resolver landed in packages/pi-subagent/src/resolve.ts with 22 tests. Preflight probe: landed, deduplicated per distinct non-session model per run, falling back to the session model with a note and re-resolving thinking against that fallback.

title: ADR: Effect as the one dependency, read-only children, graph delegation
description:
Record the decisions before the code, the way the sibling packages' ADRs do.
Written once, so the reasoning survives.

Identity: npm pi-subagent, unscoped, 0.1.0, command /subagent. Ships raw
TypeScript through jiti, no build step.

DEPENDENCY

- Effect v4 core only, the single runtime dependency. The repo rule moved from
  zero dependencies to fewest for this package, and AGENTS.md now says so.
- Core only, not the platform packages. effect/Schema is in core, so the
  settings file gets a real decoder without a second package. node:fs and
  pi.exec cover the rest, and pi.exec is required anyway for anything Pi
  should see.
- typebox stays a peer regardless, because registerTool takes a TSchema.
- Effect reaches to the tool boundary and stops. Services, Layers and Scope
  for the manager, runs and latches. One ManagedRuntime built at activation,
  and each tool execute bridges with runPromise. TUI components stay plain
  classes, because Pi's Component contract is a synchronous render(width) that
  repaints several times a second.

CHILDREN

- Read-only: read, grep, find, ls plus fff. No bash, edit or write, so no
  worktrees, no branches, no crash-recovery sweep and no merge story. That is
  the single largest cut against pi-core-subagent, which spends 366 lines
  there.
- Exactly one extension loads, @ff-labs/pi-fff, through noExtensions: true
  plus additionalExtensionPaths. Verified against Pi's compiled loader, where
  those two resolve on separate paths and noExtensions only drops the
  discovered set. Loading everything and filtering would be worse, because
  extensionsOverride runs after every factory has already executed.
- Nesting is impossible by construction, since this extension is never in a
  child's extension set. Keep the AsyncLocalStorage re-entry guard anyway as
  fifteen lines of insurance. The failure it prevents is a second manager and
  leaked handlers, which is silent and permanent.
- Standalone system prompt: Pi's base layers, then the inline prompt the
  orchestrator wrote, then the subagent instruction block. The parent's prompt
  is not inherited. A research child does not need the parent's coding
  conventions, and inheriting costs real input tokens per child.
- Sessions are persisted and nested under the parent, so /resume sees them and
  each has a path to tail. That path is what replaces the peek pane.

DELEGATION

- tasks with an optional needs list. One wave scheduler covers single,
  parallel and chain. Ordering is a schema feature from the start, because
  changing a tool schema later means the orchestrating model relearns it.
- The model invents the agent per call. A user .md applies only when addressed
  by exact name. No catalog, so no per-request context cost. Description
  matching is rejected: pi-core-subagent's version is a two-token, 40 percent
  coverage threshold over crude stemming, which surprises people both when it
  fires and when it does not.
- Four tools: subagent, subagent_result, reply_subagent, subagent_cancel.
  Status merges into result, because a dead-on-spawn failure is delivered as
  an interrupting steer, which is what a separate status tool was
  compensating for.
- ask_parent and notify_parent, no sibling mailbox. needs edges already carry
  ordered coordination, and same-wave siblings are independent by
  construction.

CONTROL

- Precedence for model and thinking: agent file, then the settings menu, then
  the per-task field, then the parent's model. Both user sources outrank the
  orchestrator's runtime guess, and the more specific user source wins. The
  setting ships as inherit, so the per-task field still works until the user
  names something concrete.
- Thinking levels come from pi-ai's own getSupportedThinkingLevels(model). Do
  not hand-roll it. A missing key in thinkingLevelMap means provider default,
  so minimal through high are opt-out, while xhigh and max are opt-in and a
  missing key excludes them. reasoning: false collapses everything to off. A
  model with no map and reasoning: true supports off, minimal, low, medium and
  high.
- Validate every task's model and level pair before any fiber forks, and
  refuse the whole call naming the task. Then also read session.thinkingLevel
  back and surface it when it differs. Validation covers what thinkingLevelMap
  describes, and reading back covers whatever it does not.
- Turn limit primary at 30 turns with 5 grace turns, wall clock as a 30 minute
  backstop. Both references default turns to unlimited, which leaves the clock
  doing all the work and lets a broken tool loop burn for hours.

ACCOUNTING

- Two token totals, both accumulated from message_end rather than session
  stats, which reset at compaction. The display total excludes cacheRead,
  because each turn's value is the cumulative prefix re-read on that one call,
  so summing counts it once per turn. The billing total includes it.
- The parent session's own cost is untouched. Pushing spend there is additive
  later and changes no schema.

Emit session_shutdown before disposing a child session. Pi emits it in its own
dispose path, and this is one of the few places that binds extensions onto a
session without going through that path. pi-fff starts an interval status poll
under some conditions, so skipping the emit leaks one interval per spawn.

title: Settings: the four-row menu and its persisted file
description:
The /subagent settings menu, plus the file behind it.

Four rows, built on pi-tui's SettingsList:

- Default model. inherit, or a concrete pick from modelRegistry.getAvailable(),
  which is already filtered to providers with configured auth. Opens a submenu,
  since the list is long.
- Default thinking effort. The values list is getSupportedThinkingLevels() for
  whichever model row one resolves to, recomputed when that row changes. A
  model row left on inherit resolves against the parent's current model.
- Concurrency. Numeric.
- Default max turns. Numeric.

SettingItem carries a values array for cycling and a submenu for anything
else. There is no dedicated numeric row, so the two numbers go through a
submenu or through ui.input.

Persist to <cwd>/.pi/subagent.json, decoded with effect/Schema. A corrupt file
falls back to defaults and notifies rather than taking the extension load with
it, and an out-of-range field is dropped while the rest still load. A settings
file is not worth a failed load.

Everything here applies live. Nothing is read at tool registration, which is
what would otherwise require a new Pi session to take effect.
close_reason: Four-row panel on SettingsList, per-field Schema decode, Effect Settings service behind a ManagedRuntime. 47 tests; three guards mutation-checked.

title: pi-subagent: read-only delegation on a dependency graph, with user-picked models
description:
A third subagent extension for Pi, built from a read of the two that exist.
Both are vendored in this repo and written up under docs/: pi-core-subagent
(3,300 lines, zero dependencies, 7 tools, a wave scheduler over needs edges)
and pi-subagents (21,000 lines, 4 dependencies, Claude Code parity plus a
scripted workflow sandbox).

This takes the graph from the first and the accounting discipline from the
second, and cuts everything neither of them proved was worth its code.

One call takes tasks with an optional needs list. No edges means plain
parallel. An edge gates the dependent and prepends the upstream output into
its prompt, so the orchestrator cannot forget to pass a result it never
passes. Children are read-only, so there are no worktrees, no branches and no
merge story. A child gets Pi's read, grep, find and ls plus fff, and nothing
else loads. The user picks the subagent model and thinking effort from a
settings menu, and the orchestrator's per-task model only applies while that
setting stays on inherit.

Scale target: under 2,500 source lines.

Deliberately out of scope, each considered and cut: write agents and the
worktree machinery they need, nested spawning, scheduling, a scripted workflow
sandbox, handle-based addressing, cross-extension RPC, structured output,
parent conversation inheritance, sidecar run history, and a peek pane.

The known risk in that shape: read-only children plus needs edges can only
chain research into synthesis. A plan-then-implement chain is not expressible,
because the implementer would need write tools. If that turns out to be the
job, write agents come back and they bring worktrees with them.

title: Wire the extension entry, lifecycle and repaint triggers
description:
index.ts, from 268 lines to about 150.

- Load config, build the widget store, register the footer through
  ctx.ui.setFooter, publish our own status key.
- Collect data per render: model, provider, thinking level (only when the
  model reports reasoning support), context usage, cwd, session metrics, git.
- Repaint on three signals: the thinking_level_select event, footerData's
  onBranchChange, and the git cache landing fresh data. The first is new.
  Upstream never subscribes to it, so under upstream a level change shows only
  on the next unrelated redraw, which would make the color feature look
  broken.
- session_start reloads config and reapplies. session_shutdown clears the
  footer and the status. model_select reapplies.
- No footer when ctx.hasUI is false or the config is disabled: clear both the
  footer and the status.
- Dispose must unsubscribe the branch listener and drop the captured
  requestRender and status accessor, as upstream does.

Gone from the entry: the before_provider_request verbosity capture, the
model_select verbosity reset, the getTextVerbosity and readTextVerbosity
helpers, and the event-widget listener.

No timers anywhere. total-time is accurate whenever the footer draws and
occasionally stale between draws, which beats repainting every second for the
whole session.

title: Port the session metrics collector
description:
metrics.ts, 141 lines, essentially verbatim.

Walks the session branch accumulating input, output, cache read and cache
write tokens, cost, message counts by role, compaction count, and first and
last timestamps. Feeds cost, total-time and the context widgets.

Keep the loose structural projections (UsageLike, MessageLike) with unknown
fields validated at runtime, and keep the comment saying why: the shapes are
Pi's session entries, and defensive parsing survives upstream changes that
derived SDK types would not.

Turn metrics stay too. cost reads session totals, but the collector computes
both and they cost one pass.
notes: Scope shrank with the widget port: SessionMetrics is now costUsd plus firstTimestampMs only, and TurnMetrics is gone. No shipped widget reads token counts, message counts by role, compactions or per-turn totals, so the collector only needs the session cost and the earliest timestamp.

title: Port git collection, fetching only what enabled widgets need
description:
git.ts plus cache.ts. The one place this diverges from upstream on purpose.

Upstream runs 7 subprocesses per refresh on a 2 second cache, kicked off from
the render path, whenever any git widget is enabled. Two of those commands
feed widgets this package does not ship.

Derive the command set from the enabled git widgets instead:

  default and compact -> rev-parse --show-toplevel, diff --shortstat
                         (branch arrives free from footerData.getGitBranch,
                          which Pi already fs-watches)
  git-heavy           -> the above plus rev-parse --short HEAD,
                         status --porcelain=v1,
                         rev-list --left-right --count @{upstream}...HEAD
  never               -> remote get-url origin

Keep the rest as it is: pi.exec with a 500ms timeout, stale-while-revalidate
so a render never blocks, requestRender when fresh data lands, and the 2 second
TTL.

Keep upstream's trimEnd comment. status --porcelain=v1 encodes staged versus
unstaged in columns 1 and 2, so trim() would strip the leading space of the
first line and miscount that file.

Test the porcelain, shortstat and ahead/behind parsers against real command
output, and test that a git-heavy config asks for more commands than a compact
one.

title: Port the render pipeline and the extension status row
description:
render.ts, roughly 100 lines, plus a trimmed extension-statuses.ts at about
25.

- Render each configured line, filter out empty ones, join segments with the
  configured separator, and skip the separator when either neighbor is itself
  a separator.
- flex-separator splits a line into left and right, padded to width.
- Every line goes through truncateToWidth with an ellipsis. Drop the
  effectiveWidth branch along with the width mode.
- Append other extensions' statuses as a final dimmed line, sorted, excluding
  our own status key. Read-only: no hiddenKeys, no knownKeys, no picker, no
  normalizer. An extension that publishes a status while pi-statusbar owns the
  footer stays visible instead of disappearing with no explanation.

Cover the cases that actually break: a line whose widgets all render empty, a
flex line with an empty right side, and truncation landing mid escape
sequence.

title: Thinking-level color: theme colors with a guarded fallback
description:
The feature the fork exists for. The thinking segment colors itself by level.

Map each level to the theme color Pi already uses for it, so the footer agrees
with Pi's own thinking indicator:

  off -> thinkingOff, minimal -> thinkingMinimal, low -> thinkingLow,
  medium -> thinkingMedium, high -> thinkingHigh, xhigh -> thinkingXhigh,
  max -> thinkingMax

Then guard it. theme.fg throws on a color the loaded theme does not define,
and from Pi 0.84 both thinkingMax and searchMatchText are optional, so a
direct lookup crashes the footer on a theme that omits thinkingMax. Two
fallback layers:

  fg = themeColor(level) if it resolves
       else FALLBACK[level]   (brightBlack, blue, cyan, yellow, magenta, red,
                               brightRed)
       else options.fg

The second layer also covers the command path, where no Theme object exists at
all.

Do not use theme.getThinkingBorderColor. It returns a colorizer function

Written once, so the reasoning survives the code.

Identity: npm pi-statusbar, unscoped, 0.1.0, command /statusbar. Ships raw

Decisions to record with their evidence:
- Port and strip rather than rewrite. The proven parts are the render
  pipeline, the git cache and the metrics parser.
- Peer >=0.80, backed by the .d.ts diff. Note the one real change found:
  0.80.6 requires every theme color, while 0.84 made thinkingMax and
  searchMatchText optional. That is exactly why the thinking color needs a
  fallback rather than a direct theme lookup.
- Colors trimmed to named ANSI16 plus pi:<themeColor>. chalk goes because the
  repo forbids runtime dependencies, and every ansi256 value upstream lives in

  same.

  anything that is not ENOENT, so a corrupt file stops the extension loading
  and takes the footer with it. A statusline is not worth a failed load.

  payload-sniffing hook, event widgets, width mode, minimalist.

title: Add timeout: the one feature rpiv does not have
description:
The only node in this design that emits over time. Everything else is a pure
reducer fed by keystrokes, so the clock stays outside it.

Schema: optional `timeout` in milliseconds on the tool parameters, described so
the model knows it auto-dismisses.

TUI path, hand-built because `ui.custom` takes no timeout:
- The session owns an unref'd `setInterval(1s)` dispatching `{ kind: "tick",
  now }`. `now` is passed IN; `reduce` never reads the clock itself, so it stays
  pure and testable.
- `reduce` computes remaining from `deadline - now`. Above zero it updates
  `state.remainingMs`; at or below zero it goes through `doneFor` with
  `cancelled: true` and `error: "timed_out"`.
- The first keystroke of any kind means a human is present: the reducer sets
  `timerCancelled` and emits a new `{ kind: "clear_timer" }` effect. Cancelled
  outright, not reset.
- Both the footer hint and the collapsed one-line row show the remaining
  seconds. A dialog you deliberately collapsed must not vanish silently.

RPC path: free. Pi's `ExtensionUIDialogOptions` already has `timeout?: number`
documented as auto-dismissing with a live countdown, in both 0.80.6 and 0.84.4.
Pass it through to `select` and `input`. Do not build a second countdown.

`timed_out` is a NEW member of `QuestionnaireError`, never folded into
`cancelled`, for the same reason `no_custom_ui` is separate: a timeout is not a
decline and the model must not treat it as one.

One action, one state field, one effect. The unions stay closed, so the
compiler still forces exhaustive handling in both the reducer table and
`runEffect`.

New tests: expiry fires `timed_out`; a keystroke cancels the timer permanently;
the countdown renders in the footer and in the collapsed row; RPC passes the
value through; no timer at all when `timeout` is absent.
close_reason: Timeout implemented: optional timeout on tool params, tick/clear_timer, live countdown in footer and collapsed row, RPC passthrough, distinct timed_out envelope. 746 tests green.

title: Wire tool registration, extension entry and lifecycle reconciler
description:
The integration bead. Everything above meets Pi here.

- `reconcile.ts`: a `before_agent_start` hook stripping `ask_user_question` from

  honest signal.
- `src/index.ts`: register the tool and the reconciler. No i18n registration.
- Terminal bell: one `\x07` to stdout immediately before the interactive wait,
  gated on `process.stdout.isTTY`. To stdout and not `/dev/tty`, so a piped RPC
  transport never rings for a dialog rendering in a remote host's own UI. Best
  effort; a failed write must not stop the questionnaire.

Lazy loading WITHOUT the prewarm timer, but keeping both guards:
- import fails -> `session_load_failed` envelope
- import resolves without the class -> `stale_module_cache` envelope
jiti is pinned at 2.7.0 in 0.84.4, so this failure is still reachable. Both
envelopes must tell the model the user never saw the questions and to ask in
chat instead, and must never look like a decline.

`.listener.test.ts` (286), `.guidance.test.ts` (142), `.session-load.test.ts`.

- Guidance reads the GLOBAL config layer only. Registration has no ctx, so

- Config warnings are held and reported on first execute via ctx.ui.notify,

- NEW GUARD: a host with hasUI true but neither ctx.ui.custom nor the dialog

title: Port RPC/ACP dialog walker
description:
Makes the tool work in Zed, Paseo and the VS Code pendant, where `ui.custom`
cannot render but the native select/input dialogs can. Needs only the tool
contract, so it does not wait on the view layer.

- `rpc-fallback.ts`: `hasDialogUI` and `runRpcQuestionnaire`, walking one
  question per dialog in order and returning the same result envelope the TUI
  produces.
- Multi-select is a free-text input taking comma-separated option numbers
  (`1,3`). Any token that is not a valid index is treated as a typed custom
  answer, which is how the "Type something." escape survives. Empty input
  commits an empty selection, matching `Next` with nothing toggled.
- Previews fold into the dialog title, truncated at 600 characters each.
- Dismissing any dialog cancels the whole questionnaire, mirroring Esc.
- Notes do not exist on this path. Both kinds are terminal-only; the native
  primitives carry no note field. Document that, do not fake it.

Two routes reach here: hosts advertising `ctx.mode === "rpc"` go straight to the
walker and skip the TUI import entirely, and older RPC builds are caught by the
backstop when `ui.custom` resolves undefined. A TUI questionnaire ALWAYS
resolves a result including cancel, so `undefined` uniquely means "host cannot
render" and must never be read as a decline.

Tests ported: `rpc-fallback.test.ts` (273).

Landed as "Port the RPC dialog walker".

src/rpc-fallback.ts: hasDialogUI + runRpcQuestionnaire. Ported from upstream
with i18n removed (the sentinel row label now comes from ROW_INTENT_META.other,
same source the overlay row uses) and the preview key switched to a conditional
spread so a preview-free answer keeps the "absent, not undefined" contract.

ask_user_question.execute -- mode routing, the BEL, the blocked events, and the
custom()-undefined backstop. Those are all wiring decisions, so they are left

directly: 35 tests.

third ExtensionUIDialogOptions arg carrying signal and timeout. The structural
DialogUI type declares two parameters, which is assignable, and the timeout
bead can widen it in one line when it needs to pass opts.

confirmed rather than assumed:
- "await (a ? f() : g())" vs "a ? await f() : await g()" is the same program.
  A genuine Promise.all rewrite IS killed by the sequencing test.
- The empty-multi-input early return is observationally identical to falling
  through: no tokens makes indices.every() vacuously true, producing the same
  empty selection. Kept explicit anyway, with a comment saying why, so nobody

title: Port questionnaire session, builder and external editor
description:
The runtime that owns the state cell and runs effects. The only impure edge in
the design.

- `state/questionnaire-session.ts`: holds canonical state, the two headless
  `Editor` instances, the notes-draft mirror, and the `runEffect` switch.
- `state/build-questionnaire.ts`: the builder assembling every component, the
  props adapter and the lifecycle handle.
- `state/external-editor.ts`: the `Ctrl+G` round trip through Pi's configured
  external editor.

Details that are load-bearing:
- Both editors set `disableSubmit = true`. Without it, a `tui.input.submit`
  match inside `Editor.handleInput` runs `submitValue()`, which resets the
  buffer. No `onSubmit` is wired, so the draft is unrecoverable.
- The notes mirror reads `getExpandedText()` before `getText()`, so restoring a
  draft through `setText` never orphans a paste marker.
- Collapse emits `set_overlay_hidden` ONLY when `canReopenWhileHidden` is true.
  Pi routes no input to a hidden overlay, so a host with an OverlayHandle but no
  raw terminal input would otherwise hide the dialog into a state nothing can
  reopen. That host gets the visible one-line collapsed row instead.
- While the external editor is open, input dispatch is suspended.

Tests ported: `questionnaire-session.test.ts`, `external-editor.test.ts`,
`factory.test.ts` (1103).
notes:
Landed as "Port the questionnaire session, builder and external editor".

Files: state/questionnaire-session.ts, state/build-questionnaire.ts,
state/external-editor.ts. i18n removed throughout; WrappingSelectItem now comes
from state/row-intent.

Two source changes beyond the port:
- external-editor validates an empty/whitespace command BEFORE tui.stop().
  Upstream checked inside runEditor, after the handover, so a misconfigured
  EDITOR flashed the screen off and back on.
- build-questionnaire throws on zero questions rather than a non-null
  assertion, which would have failed as a property access during first paint.
- injectGlobalLeftWidth passes `questions` directly as the tab descriptor
  instead of mapping to { multiSelect }, which produced an explicit undefined
  that exactOptionalPropertyTypes rejects.

New suite for the builder (upstream had none -- it was only reachable through
registerAskUserQuestionTool). Eight wiring decisions were invisible from there:
disableSubmit on both editors, separate buffers, the shared cross-tab left
column, tab bar only when multi, multi-select view only when the question is,
notesInput in extraInvalidatables, collapse key threading, and the empty-input
refusal.

Testing note for later beads: rendering a real PreviewPane needs initTheme()
from pi-coding-agent, otherwise pi-tui's Markdown throws on heading styles. The
builder suite calls it in beforeAll. Do NOT mock Markdown instead -- that is
what let three mutations survive in the preview layer.

- tab bar built for a single question is never rendered (isMulti gates it)
- the second-launch guard inside openInputEditorAsync sits behind an
  already-suspended dispatch; unreachable defensive depth
- committing state after the effect loop is unobservable; no effect reads state

  which is an unhandled rejection the suite cannot observe. Verified that

  ever grows.
The fifth was real: an unclaimed keystroke while browsing rows. Focusing the
custom row restores its draft, so stray text never reaches an answer -- but it
does cost a render per keystroke, which is now asserted.

title: Rewrite config loader for Pi's extension settings convention
description:
Replaces `@juicesharp/rpiv-config` with about 50 lines we own. Independent of
the state and view work; can run in parallel with the port.

Locations, per Pi's documented convention rather than rpiv's XDG path:
- `<getAgentDir()>/pi-ask-popup.json`
- `<workspace>/<CONFIG_DIR_NAME>/pi-ask-popup.json` overriding it

Semantics, mirroring Pi core:
- An absent file means no overrides. Reading must NOT create the file or its
  parent directory.
- Defaults live in code.
- A malformed file falls back to defaults with a warning and never becomes an
  error. An individual unusable value is silently dropped to its default.
- Storage errors stay data until the caller reports them. Never print directly:
  this process is also speaking JSON-RPC on some hosts.

Fields: `collapseKey`, and `guidance.{description,promptSnippet,promptGuidelines}`.
Timeout is NOT here; it is a tool parameter.

Port `resolveCollapseKey` and its strict KeyId grammar unchanged. The strictness
matters: pi-tui's `parseKeyId` takes the last `+`-part as the base key and
ignores unknown parts, so a typo like `ctr+]` would silently bind every bare
`]` keypress and the raw terminal listener would then eat them globally.
Keep `formatKeySpecForDisplay` and the `"off"` sentinel.

Tests: rewrite `config.test.ts` against the new locations, including the
project-override precedence which rpiv had no equivalent of.
notes:
Landed as "Add the config loader".

Shape: loadConfig({ agentDir, projectDir? }) -> { config, warnings }. Directories
are arguments, not import-time resolution, so tests use a temp dir instead of
mutating HOME (upstream's own test carries a comment about fighting that).
Project layer is skipped unless the caller passes a dir -- that is where
ctx.isProjectTrusted() lands, per Pi's extensions doc.

Divergences from upstream, both verified against pi-tui 0.84.4 source:
- `"` removed from the accepted symbol set. pi-tui's SYMBOL_KEYS has no double
  quote, so ctrl+" validated and then matched nothing. Confirmed by running
  matchesKey over the printable range.
- `+` removed; it is the separator and matchesKey("+","+") is false.
- parseKeyId confirmed to take the last +-part and only ask whether the rest
  *include* a known modifier, so the ctr+] hazard is real as documented.

Warnings are returned as data, never printed. Guidance merges per field.

Mutation-tested, 8 mutations, all now fail at least one test: merge order
reversed, backslash dropped from the symbol set, `"` re-added, ENOENT warning,
guidance replace-instead-of-merge, unknown modifiers accepted, array config
accepted, digits rejected. Plus a mkdir injected into the read path to prove
the never-creates guard is falsifiable.

One mutation initially survived: dropping the backslash. Cause was the test
hand-typing its own symbol list, which lost the escape exactly as the source
did. Fixed by enumerating candidates by codepoint and deriving the expected
answer from matchesKey at run time.

460 tests, 19 files, full gate green.

title: Port tool contract layer: schema, row intent, validation, envelope
description:
First code to land. No UI, no state, pure data and validation.

- `tool/types.ts`: typebox schema, MAX_QUESTIONS 4, MIN/MAX_OPTIONS 2/4,

  `QuestionnaireResult`, `QuestionnaireError`.
- `state/row-intent.ts`: the `ROW_INTENT_META` table. Keep the
  `Record<RowKind, ...>` shape so adding a sentinel fails to compile until
  every consumer is updated. That property is the reason this table exists.
- `tool/validate-questionnaire.ts`, `tool/format-answer.ts`,
  `tool/response-envelope.ts`.
- Reserved labels stay `["Other", "Type something.", "Next"]`. `"Other"` is

DONE. src/tool/{types,validate-questionnaire,format-answer,response-envelope}.ts
and src/state/row-intent.ts, with every i18n call site replaced by its English
literal. 84 tests across 5 files, green under both vitest and bun test.

DESIGN CHANGE, deliberate: the row-kind dependency is inverted. Upstream derived
RowKind from the view layer's WrappingSelectItem union, which would have forced
the view to exist before the protocol. RowKind now lives in row-intent.ts and
the view will build its item type from it. Intent belongs to the protocol, not
the renderer, and the compile-time forcing gets STRONGER: adding a kind breaks
the Record<RowKind, ...> metadata AND every exhaustive switch in the renderer.
The view-layer work must build WrappingSelectItem from RowKind, not redeclare it.

Also inverted: SentinelKind is re-exported from row-intent rather than
redefined in types.ts. Upstream had two structurally identical definitions of
the same type in two modules, which is a drift hazard for no benefit.

Tests written beyond the plan. Upstream has no dedicated suites for the
validator or the envelope; that logic is covered indirectly by the
tool-registration tests, which land several steps later. Both modules have real
branching, so they got their own suites now rather than arriving untested:
validate-questionnaire.test.ts and response-envelope.test.ts. banned-flags is
folded into row-intent.test.ts as "discriminator discipline", scoped to src/,
with a guard asserting the file walk is non-empty so the check cannot pass by
scanning nothing.

reserved-label check MUST precede the duplicate-label check. Mutation testing
disproved it: swapping the two blocks left all 84 tests green. The orderings are
observationally equivalent for every possible input, because a reserved label
trips on its FIRST occurrence, when seenLabels cannot yet contain it. Two
"Other" options therefore return reserved_label at index 0 under either order,
and index 1 is unreachable. No option can ever be both reserved and a duplicate.

The test asserting that precedence was consequently tautological and has been
rewritten to say what it actually pins, with the reasoning recorded in the
source comment plus an instruction not to re-add a precedence test.

Mutation testing also confirmed a real invariant holds: moving the
segments-empty check above the global-note append correctly failed
"treats a global note with no answers as answered, not declined", and only that.

builtins only, no bun: APIs, @types/node not @types/bun. A bare `bun test` from
the repo root walks the vendored clones and hangs, hence the scoped path.

Committed as 679ca53.

title: ADR: fork rpiv-ask-user-question as zero-dep pi-ask-popup
description:
Decisions settled before any code, with the evidence behind them.

## Identity
- npm `pi-ask-popup`, unscoped, starts at 0.1.0. Verified free on npm;
  `pi-ask-user` is taken by a similar package (edlsh, MIT, zero deps).
- New directory `pi-ask-popup/`, single package, `git init`, no remote yet, so
  `repository` and `homepage` stay out of package.json until one exists.
- Author `derangga <derangga1011@gmail.com>`. LICENSE is MIT carrying
  juicesharp's original copyright line plus derangga's, as the MIT terms
  require of a fork.
- Ships raw TypeScript. `"pi": { "extensions": ["./src/index.ts"] }`, jiti
  loads it. No build, no dist. Layout `src/` + `test/`.

## Dependencies
- Zero runtime dependencies. Peers only: `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent >=0.80`,
  `@earendil-works/pi-tui >=0.80`, `typebox *`.
- Peer is `typebox`, NOT `@sinclair/typebox`. Pi 0.84.4 depends on typebox@1.3.7.
  `pi-ask-user` peer-declares the old name; do not copy that.
- No Effect. Rejected: effect@3.22.1 is 27 MB unpacked, larger than Pi's own
  coding agent (21 MB), against a zero-dep goal and a 114 kB competitor. Effect
  v4, which the house style targets, is still 4.0.0-rc.112 with no stable
  release. The code has three async edges total. Failure is modeled as tagged
  unions instead: Effect-shaped, no import.

## Pi compatibility (verified by diffing the published .d.ts of both versions)
- `ui.select`, `ui.input`, `ui.custom`, `ui.onTerminalInput`, `ctx.mode`,
  `ctx.hasUI` are identical in 0.80.6 and 0.84.4.
- `OverlayHandle` (hide/setHidden/isHidden/focus/unfocus) is byte-identical at
  the same line numbers in pi-tui 0.80.6 and 0.84.4, so collapse mode ports
  untouched.
- 137 changed lines elsewhere in `core/extensions/types.d.ts` between versions,
  none in the surface this package uses. `>=0.80` is therefore safe.
- `ExtensionUIDialogOptions` already carries `timeout?: number`, documented as
  "auto-dismisses with live countdown display", in BOTH versions. The RPC path
  gets timeout as a pass-through; only the TUI overlay needs a hand-built clock.

## Kept
Pure reducer and key router, tabbed multi-question dialog, Submit review tab,
side-by-side markdown previews, multi-select with the `Next` row, the appended
`Type something.` row, per-question and global notes, collapse mode on
`Ctrl+]`, the RPC/ACP dialog walker, the `no_ui` / `no_custom_ui` /
`session_load_failed` / `stale_module_cache` envelopes, and every test covering
a surviving feature.

## Dropped
`@juicesharp/rpiv-config`, `@juicesharp/rpiv-i18n`, the i18n bridge, nine locale
files, `locales.test.ts`, `i18n-bridge.shim.test.ts`, `ship-manifest.test.ts`,
typebox as a hard dependency, and the 2-second prewarm timer.

The two load-failure envelopes STAY even though prewarm goes: jiti is pinned at
2.7.0 in both 0.80.6 and 0.84.4, so the cache-poisoning bug they guard against
(a failed import stays registered in the graph cache and poisons every later
import for the process lifetime) is still live in the targeted version.

## Added
`timeout`. Distinct `timed_out` error, never folded into `cancelled`, for the
same reason `no_custom_ui` is distinct: a timeout is not a decline and the
model must not read it as one.

## Out of scope
No Effect. No searchable option filter (the schema caps options at four). No
cross-session answer memory. No cover art. No CI. No changesets. No built
`dist/`. No raised caps on questions or options.

## Open question, deliberately deferred
`"Other"` stays in the reserved-label list purely because Claude Code
conditions models to reach for it. Worth keeping only as long as tool-name
parity is the goal.
notes:
AMENDMENT (supersedes the "Identity" section's single-package decision):

The repo hosts 4-5 Pi extensions, not one. It is an npm-workspaces monorepo
rooted at /Users/sociolla/Documents/playground/pi-extension, and pi-ask-popup
lives at packages/pi-ask-popup. Everything else in this ADR stands unchanged:
independently versioned, independently published, zero runtime dependencies,
raw TypeScript with no build.

Consequences worth recording:

- Shared tooling lives at the root: package.json workspaces, tsconfig.base.json,
  .oxlintrc.json, .oxfmtrc.json, vitest.config.ts. Each package extends the base
  tsconfig and owns its own package.json, README and LICENSE.
- Pi peer dependencies are ALSO root devDependencies pinned at 0.84.4, so every
  package typechecks against one version while peering the wider >=0.80 range.
- Every root script is scoped to `packages/` (`oxlint packages`, `oxfmt
  packages`, vitest include `packages/*/test/**/*.test.ts`). Not cosmetic: the
  repo root also holds vendored reference clones with thousands of their own
  source and test files, and an unscoped glob would lint and run all of them.
- The vendored clones (pi-extensions, pi-footer, rpiv-mono) are excluded via
  .git/info/exclude, NOT .gitignore, at the user's instruction. That file is
  local to this clone and is never itself tracked, so the exclusion cannot leak
  into anyone else's checkout. Beads already used the same mechanism for its
  Dolt files, so this is consistent with what was there.

npm run check clean.

title: Docs and README
description:
README covering install, the tool surface, the four settings rows, the
precedence rules for model and thinking effort, what a child can and cannot do,
and the one runtime dependency with the reason it earns its place, which
AGENTS.md now requires of every package that has one.

Position it against the two prior extensions honestly. Both are vendored in this
repo and written up under docs/. Say what this one cut and why, including the
risk named in the epic: read-only children mean a plan-then-implement chain is
not expressible here.

Document the shape of a child's context, since that is the thing users get
wrong. A child sees the task text plus any upstream outputs, and nothing of the
parent conversation.

title: Usage accounting and the three lifecycle events
description:
Accumulate from message_end, never from getSessionStats(), which derives from
the message array that compaction replaces and so resets every time a child
compacts.

Two totals from one accumulator. The display total is input plus output plus
cacheWrite. The billing total adds cacheRead. Both are real answers to different
questions: each turn's cacheRead is the cumulative cached prefix re-read on that
one call, so summing it overstates work done while stating the bill correctly.

Cost comes from Pi's own per-message cost total. Nothing is priced here. A model
Pi has no rates for contributes zero, and zero prints nothing rather than a
zero-dollar figure, which would claim the run was measured and found free. A
real cost too small to render prints as less than the smallest displayable
figure instead of rounding to nothing.

The parent session's own totals stay untouched. A delegating session will read
as cheaper than it was, which is the accepted trade for not building the pending
usage pool yet.

Three events on the bus: run-started, task-settled and run-settled, carrying
ids, status and usage. Enough for pi-statusbar or anything else to render run
state without importing this package. No RPC and no spawn-from-outside surface
until something actually asks for one.

title: The typed colors subcommand, usage and settings summary
description:
The typed form, the usage line and the settings summary.

Every other setting is reachable from the prompt, so a scheme should be too:
it keeps the pattern, and it is the only way to script one.

Named "colors" and not "theme", matching the row. The word theme belongs to
the Pi-wide setting this feature does not touch.

The usage says <name> with a pointer that the bare command lists them, rather
than spelling out twelve names. The separator line already lists its seven
styles inline and is at the limit of what fits.

describeSettings gains the scheme, so the headless summary and the bare
command under NO_COLOR both say which one is active.
acceptance_criteria:
- /statusbar colors <name> sets a scheme; every one of the twelve parses.
- An unknown name warns with the usage text and changes nothing, matching
  every other bad argument.
- The usage names the subcommand without listing all twelve schemes.
- describeSettings names the active scheme.
- No usage line wraps at 80 columns.

title: The Color scheme row and its picker
description:
The Color scheme row, and the picker it opens.

Called "Color scheme" and not "Theme". It does not change Pi's theme, which
lives in /settings; a row named Theme would send someone to report that
picking github-light failed to restyle their editor.

Enter opens a picker rather than the arrows cycling in place, breaking the
pattern the other rows follow. Thirteen entries is too many to arrow through
one repaint at a time, and pi-tui's SettingItem.submenu supports a submenu
component directly.

  Color scheme   catppuccin-mocha >

    v default          (follow Pi's theme)
      ayu-dark         ######
      catppuccin-latte ######  light
      catppuccin-mocha ######
      tokyo-night      ######

Each row is painted in its own scheme and carries a swatch, so all thirteen
can be compared without moving the cursor, and the light ones announce
themselves rather than surprising someone on a dark terminal.

Moving the cursor repaints the real footer and writes nothing. Enter commits;
escape restores the scheme the picker opened with, in memory. This is the one
place the panel has a notion of current that differs from what is saved, and
it is deliberate: browsing thirteen schemes must not cost thirteen writes, and
escape has to mean no change here, the way it does everywhere else.
acceptance_criteria:
- Enter on the row opens the picker; the arrows do not cycle it in place.
- The active entry is marked with a plain check, U+2713, fixed regardless of
  the icon set, since the picker is panel chrome and not footer content.
- Each entry is painted in its own scheme and shows a swatch; light-terminal
  schemes are labelled.
- Moving the cursor repaints the footer and produces no commit and no write.
  Proven by asserting the commit count, not by inspection.
- Enter commits exactly one change. Escape commits none and leaves the footer
  on the scheme the picker opened with.
- Thirteen entries scroll rather than overflowing a short terminal.
- Driven by real keystrokes through the real component, extending the existing
  panel-keys pattern.

title: The scheme owns the thinking ladder, the dim row and the separator
description:
Hand the thinking ladder, the dim status row and the separator to the scheme.

These three are the only places that resolve a pi: token rather than a named
color, so a scheme would sail straight past them. Pi's built-in dark theme
defines every thinkingLevel token and dim, so on a stock install the result
would be a catppuccin footer with one segment and one whole row visibly from a
different palette.

The thinking ladder matters most: its color is the package's headline feature,
so it must not be the one segment that looks foreign.

The dim row is other extensions' text, which is the argument for leaving it on
Pi's theme. Overruled deliberately: while a scheme is active the whole footer
is that scheme, and half a footer in each palette is worse than either.

With "default" active all three keep taking Pi's theme, exactly as now.
acceptance_criteria:
- With a scheme active, each thinking level paints that scheme's value for
  that level, not pi:thinking*. All seven levels covered.
- The dim extension-status row and the separator take the scheme's colors too.
- With "default" active, all three resolve through Pi's theme unchanged,
  including the existing fallback when a theme omits a token.
- The regression tests that prove Theme.fg is never called unguarded still
  pass: a scheme must not reintroduce a throw on a theme that defines nothing.

title: Paint widget colors through the active scheme
description:
Resolve every named widget color through the active scheme.

This is where the two previous layers become visible. The config gains the
field that names a scheme, and applyColors consults the active scheme for a
named color before falling back to the basic ANSI code it emits today.

"default" is the shipped value and means inherit: named colors and pi: tokens
behave exactly as they do now, no truecolor is emitted, and there is nothing
to regress. It is also the way back out of any scheme, and it stays correct if
Pi's theme changes later.

A name the config does not recognise falls back to "default" rather than
failing to load, the same way an unknown preset and an unknown separator
already do.

Hex stays rejected in per-widget fg. A widget names a slot and the scheme
decides what it looks like, which already gives arbitrary colors indirectly:
name brightCyan and pick a scheme. One way for color to reach the screen is
worth more than an escape hatch that no scheme can restyle.
acceptance_criteria:
- A named color renders as the scheme's hex at truecolor and as the nearest
  basic code below it.
- With "default" active, rendered output is byte-identical to today for every
  preset. Pinned by a test, since this is the whole no-regression claim.
- An unrecognised scheme name normalises to "default" and the config still
  loads.
- pi: tokens are unaffected: they still resolve through Pi's theme.
- A hex in per-widget fg is still rejected by normalizeColor.
- All 14 widget files are unchanged by this issue.

title: The twelve color schemes as data
description:
The twelve color schemes, as a typechecked table and nothing else.

A scheme redefines the color names the widgets already use, so all 14 widget
files stay untouched: each keeps naming its slot, and the scheme decides what
that slot looks like.

Each scheme carries the full 16-color ANSI palette rather than only the seven
names in use. Every upstream project publishes exactly that table, because it
is what a terminal theme is, so it is easier to source correctly and easier to
verify against the original. It also means a color hand-set in the config gets
restyled too, instead of some names changing and others not.

Seven thinking-level colors ride along, because the scheme owns that segment.

  ayu-dark              catppuccin-frappe
  ayu-light *           catppuccin-latte *
  catppuccin-macchiato  catppuccin-mocha
  github-dark           github-light *
  tokyo-night           tokyo-night-day *
  tokyo-night-moon      tokyo-night-storm

  * expects a light terminal background

Foregrounds only. A scheme never fills a background, so the footer keeps
sitting on the terminal's own and a light scheme cannot paint a bright band
across the bottom of a dark screen.

276 values sourced by hand is the part most likely to carry an error that no
test can catch. Values come from each project's published terminal palette and
get spot-checked against the original.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every scheme defines all 16 ANSI names and all 7 thinking levels; a
  completeness test walks the table rather than sampling it.
- Every value matches /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/, lowercase, so a typo in a hex is a
  test failure and not a black segment.
- Scheme names are unique, and the light-terminal ones are flagged in the data
  rather than inferred from their names.
- No scheme is wired to anything yet: this issue adds data and types only.

title: A truecolor rung on the color ladder
description:
Add a truecolor rung to the color ladder, so a hex value can reach the screen.

ColorLevel is "ansi" | "none" today, and applyColors emits only the 16 basic
codes or hands a pi: name to Pi's Theme. A color scheme is hex, so it has
nowhere to go until this exists.

The port dropped 256-color and truecolor deliberately. This brings back
truecolor and nothing else: there is still no 6x6x6 cube tier, so below
truecolor a hex maps to the nearest of the 16 basic colors. That keeps the
package's stated scope honest while making a scheme possible.

Terminal capability comes from Theme.getColorMode(), which Pi has already
decided once. Sniffing COLORTERM here would be a second opinion that can
disagree with the colors Pi paints two lines above the footer.

Nothing produces a hex yet, so this lands with no visible change.
acceptance_criteria:
- ColorLevel is "none" | "ansi" | "truecolor".
- resolveColorLevel: NO_COLOR wins over everything and still yields "none";
  Theme.getColorMode() === "truecolor" yields "truecolor"; anything else,
  including no theme at all, yields "ansi".
- applyColors emits \e[38;2;R;G;Bm for a hex at "truecolor", the nearest basic
  code at "ansi", and plain text at "none".
- nearestAnsi is pinned by a table test over known values, not by asserting
  whatever it currently returns.
- Every existing test passes untouched, since no caller emits a hex.

title: Ship 0.1.0 to npm
description:
- npm run check clean: fmt, lint, typecheck, test.
- Read the npm pack --dry-run file list line by line. src/, docs/, README,
  LICENSE. No test/, no configs, no screenshots that belong in the repo only.
- Confirm the LICENSE carries both copyright holders, upstream first. Deleting
  an upstream copyright line makes the package unlicensed.
- Verify it loads under both runtimes, since Pi ships as a Bun binary and a
  Node CLI: install the packed tarball into Pi under each and check the footer
  renders. The unit suite does not cover this, and the three places that
  actually diverge are isTTY (we avoid it), filesystem paths (the config
  loader) and dynamic import.
- Sanity-check a fresh install with no config file, then each preset, then
  NO_COLOR=1.
- publishConfig access public. Then publish.

title: README and docs
description:
Needs a working footer, since the screenshots come from it.

- README: install, the three presets with a rendered example each, the two
  icon modes, the command reference, the JSON config shape with the widget
  and option tables, and requirements.
- Document the thinking color: the level-to-theme-color mapping, that it
  follows the active Pi theme, and that it falls back to a fixed palette on a
  theme missing the color.
- Credit pi-footer as the origin, plainly and near the top, and say what this
  package is not: no powerline, no config UI, 14 widgets rather than 56. Point
  anyone who wants those upstream. Honesty costs nothing and saves people
  installing the wrong package.
- Take screenshots from your own terminal. Upstream's images live on
  wobondar's raw.githubusercontent URLs; reusing them would both break and
  misattribute.
- Note the nerd font requirement for icons nerd, and that emoji is the
  default because it needs no patched font.

title: Test suite
description:
Seven files. Upstream has 40-plus, most covering the TUI being dropped.

  manifest         packaging guards
  render           lines, flex split, separator joining, truncation
  config           normalize, presets, malformed-JSON fallback, command args
  colors           exact escape sequences, NO_COLOR, no chalk import
  thinking-color   level to color, plus the fallback when a fake theme throws
                   on thinkingMax and when no theme exists
  git              porcelain, shortstat and ahead/behind parsing, and the
                   per-preset command selection
  metrics          usage accumulation across a session branch

Swap dependencies rather than mocking the world: config path through the env
var, pi.exec through a stub, Theme through a fake plus a throwing one,
footerData through a plain object.

A test that cannot fail is not a test. For the thinking fallback and the
manifest guards especially, break the thing on purpose, watch the right test
go red and the others stay green, then revert.

title: The /statusbar command
description:
The entire config surface, in place of upstream's 3,500-line TUI.

Bare /statusbar prints current state as a notification: preset, icon mode,
enabled, and the config file path. The path matters more than usual here,
since it is how someone finds the file to hand-edit.

Arguments:
  preset default|compact|git-heavy
  icons emoji|nerd
  on | off
  reset

Anything else prints usage.

Icon precedence: an explicit icons choice persists and a later preset switch
never overwrites it. Presets carry no icon hint at all. A font capability
belongs to the terminal, not to a layout.

Every mutation saves to disk and reapplies immediately. A failed write
notifies rather than throwing.

title: Ship 0.1.0 to npm
description:
Final gate.

- `prepublishOnly` green: typecheck, fmt:check, lint, tests.
- `npm pack --dry-run` reviewed file by file. `files` must ship `src/`, docs,
  README and LICENSE, and nothing else. A stray `test/` or config file in the
  tarball is the usual mistake.
- Install the packed tarball into a scratch Pi setup and actually call the tool:
  single question, four questions with tabs, multi-select, an option carrying a
  preview, notes, the global note, collapse, and a timeout expiring.
- Confirm zero `dependencies` in the published manifest.
- Verify the LICENSE carries both copyright lines.
- `npm publish --access public`.
- Then, and only then, consider a git remote, CI and a cover image. All three
  are explicitly out of scope until something is actually published.
notes:
ADD to the ship checklist: a pi-install smoke test, following pi-footer's
.github/workflows/pi-install-smoke.yml, which is the closest precedent for a
standalone published Pi extension.

Its matrix is package-manager [npm, pnpm, bun] crossed with install-method
[npm, git, raw-url, absolute-path, relative-path], on Node 22 and 24. The bun
row excludes the node-version axis, with the comment "Bun runs pi on its own
runtime, so its job name omits the node version."

This matters because Pi is distributed both ways: the npm package declares
engines node >=22.19 and a plain JS bin, while the binary distribution is
bun-compiled (bun-v1.3.13 verified embedded in the local install). An extension
is loaded into whichever the user has.

The check to run before publishing: install the packed tarball into a scratch Pi
under npm and under bun, and confirm the extension loads and the tool appears.
That is the real portability proof. Running the unit suite under a second
runtime was tried and reverted: the suite is pure logic, so it proved nothing,
and no repo in the ecosystem does it. The places that actually diverge are
process.stdout.isTTY, filesystem paths and dynamic import() — all of which land
in the config-loader and tool-registration work, and all of which this smoke
test exercises for real.

title: Write docs, retake screenshots, position against prior art
description:
Needs a working dialog, since the screenshots come from it.

- Port `docs/keyboard.md`, `docs/hosts.md`, `docs/tool-schema.md`.
- Rewrite `docs/configuration.md` for the agentDir plus workspace-override
  loader. Drop `docs/localization.md` entirely.
- Retake every screenshot from your own terminal. rpiv's images are juicesharp's
  files on their `raw.githubusercontent` URLs; reusing them would both break and
  misattribute. Until a git remote exists they ship inside the tarball, so watch
  the package size.
- README: install, quick start, the feature list, config table, requirements
  (Node 22+, 100 columns for side-by-side previews), and troubleshooting for the
  `Ctrl+]` key being unreachable on Latin American layouts.
- Positioning, stated plainly rather than implied: credit
  `@juicesharp/rpiv-ask-user-question` as the origin, and name `pi-ask-user` as
  the leaner alternative so people can choose. Honesty here costs nothing and
  buys trust from the exact audience that reads npm listings carefully.
- Every doc updated for what actually shipped: no i18n, timeout present,
  config in a new location.

title: Rename event surface and expose ./events subpath
description:
- `rpiv:ask-user:prompt` becomes `pi-ask-popup:prompt`, emitted when the
  questionnaire is put to the user, carrying question headers, option labels and
  descriptions, `multiSelect`, and a `hasPreview` boolean per option.
- The blocked event becomes `pi-ask-popup:blocked`, emitted `true` before the
  wait and `false` in a `finally`, so a listener can never be left stuck on.
- Export both names and their payload types from `src/events.ts`, exposed as an
  `"./events"` entry in package.json `exports`.

The subpath exists so a footer, statusline or notifier can subscribe to the
payload types without importing the render graph. Keep it free of any import
that reaches the view layer, or it defeats itself.
notes:
Landed as "Rename the event surface and expose it on ./events".

Channels: pi-ask-popup:prompt, pi-ask-popup:blocked. Payload builders live in
src/events.ts (buildPromptPayload, buildBlockedPayload) so the wiring bead only
has to call them and bracket the wait.

Stronger than the bead asked: the module imports NOTHING, not just nothing that
reaches the view. Importing tool/types would pull typebox into a listener that
wants four interfaces and two strings. The parameter shape is declared
structurally (PromptSource) and a test passes a real QuestionParams through
buildPromptPayload to prove the structural declaration still matches. A second
test greps the source for import/export-from lines and fails if one appears.

Preview content is deliberately excluded from the payload; only hasPreview
ships. Fields are copied individually rather than spread, so later additions to
the tool parameters cannot leak into events other processes relay.

package.json exports now: "." and "./events". The manifest suite already
asserted every export target resolves on disk; added an explicit assertion for
the subpath value too.

Mutation-tested: 10 mutations, 0 survivors, covering both channel renames,
preview leakage, the empty-preview edge, multiSelect normalization, both spread
variants, an added import, the blocked flag, and deleting the subpath from
package.json.

563 tests, 24 files, full gate green.

title: Document the color schemes
description:
Document the color schemes.

Kept separate from the package's own README issue because that one describes
0.1.0, which ships without this feature. Folding these docs in would either
block the release or leave the README describing something that is not there.

What a reader needs, and nothing else:

- That this recolors the footer and not Pi. Anyone who picks github-light and
  sees their editor unchanged has read the docs wrong, or the docs are wrong.
- The twelve names, with the light-terminal ones marked.
- That truecolor is required to see a scheme as itself, and that below it every
  scheme degrades to the basic 16 and so looks like no scheme at all. This is
  the likeliest support question.
- That "default" means inherit and is the way back.
- That per-widget fg names a slot the scheme defines, which is how to get a
  color the schemes do not offer.
acceptance_criteria:
- The README says plainly that a scheme recolors the footer, not Pi's theme,
  and points at /settings for that.
- All twelve names appear, light-terminal ones marked.
- The truecolor requirement and the degradation below it are stated, not
  implied.
- Carries no issue tracker IDs, per the repo rule.
